text:
https://www.rochester.edu/newscenter/artificial-general-intelligence-large-language-models-644892/



Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of the most popular and fastest growing technologies over the past half decade because of its wide range of uses and applications. AI can be an extremely useful tool for many different jobs, however, as it has become more widespread it has been used to replace “Human Intelligence”. In my opinion, generally, generative AI use is acceptable when it is moderate and not used for entire projects and presented as one’s own individual work. Generative AI should only be used as a helping tool to either aid with learning or assist in specific problem solving cases.

title: AI Usage
text:
My AI Use
When it comes to my school/professional work I rarely use generative AI beyond basic queries. I mainly use Large Language Models (LLM) like ChatGPT as an advanced search engine, for when my questions may be too specific to get an instant answer from Google. For example, when working on a coding project, sometimes I get errors that I have not seen before or are not easily readable, in this case I paste the error message into an LLM to get a detailed description of the error message and the common causes for it.

title: Homework 3 – Regression
text:
1.1 Part a
Fit the regression model.
\[\begin{align*}
  Y_i =& \beta_0  +
       \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 I(x_{2i}=\text{B})+ \beta_3 I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) + \beta_4 I(x_{4i}=\text{High}) +\\
       & \beta_5 x_{5i} + \beta_6 I( x_{6i}=\text{Group2}) + \beta_7 x_{7i} + \beta_8 x_{8i}+\\
       & \beta_9 (I(x_{3i}=\text{Treat}) ~\times~ I(x_{4i}=\text{High})) + \tag{Categorical $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{10} (x_{5i} ~\times~ I(x_{6i}=\text{Group2})) +\tag{Continuous $\times$ Categorical}\\
        & \beta_{11} (x_{7i} ~\times~ x_{8i}) +
         \epsilon_i \tag{Continuous $\times$ Continuous}
\end{align*}\]
Solution: First, we fit the regression model using lm().



Code

1.3 Part c
Interpret the intercept, the coefficients on \(x_1\) and \(x_2\).



Code
knitr::kable(mod.q1$coefficients[1:3])






x

The intercept (8.9) is the predicted value of the dependent variable if all of the dependent variables are 0. \(x_1\) is a continuous value so the coefficient for \(x_1\) (2.14) is how much the predicted value of the dependent variable changes when \(x_1\) changes and all other independent variables are held constant. So in this case if all dependent variables are held constant and \(x_1\) is increased by \(1\) then \(\hat{y}\) increases by (2.14). \(x_2\), however, is a categorical value so the interpretation of its coefficient is different. There are only two possible values of \(x_2\) ‘A’ or ‘B’, and the variable in the regression model is labeled \(x_2B\). This tells us that when \(x_2\) is ‘A’ \(x_2B = 0\) and when \(x_2\) is ‘B’ \(x_2B = 1\), so when \(x_2\) is ‘A’ \(\hat{y}\) does not change but when \(x_2\) is ‘B’ \(\hat{y}\) increases by 10.03.

title: Homework 3 – Regression
text:
2.1 Part a
Compute the estimates we derived using calculus in lecture 16: \[\begin{align*}
\widehat{\beta}_0 &= \bar{y} - \widehat{\beta}_1 \bar{x}_1 \\
\widehat{\beta}_1 &= \frac{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i} - \bar{x}_1)(y_i-\bar{y})}{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_{1i}-\bar{x}_1)^2}.
\end{align*}\]



Code
dat.q2 = tibble(Temperature = c(25, -25, -75, -125, -175), Strength = c(81.93, 76.63, 63.23, 32.13, 12.83))
sum1 = 0
sum2 = 0
xbar = mean(dat.q2$Temperature)
ybar = mean(dat.q2$Strength)
for(i in 1:length(dat.q2$Temperature)){
  sum1 = sum1 + ((dat.q2$Temperature[i] - xbar)*(dat.q2$Strength[i] - ybar))
  sum2 = sum2 + (dat.q2$Temperature[i] - xbar)^2
}
b1 = sum1/sum2
b0 = ybar - b1*xbar
dat.regression = tibble(method = "Calculus", b_0 = b0, b_1 = b1)



Using the calculus approach the regression model we get is \(y = 80.755 + 0.3654x_1\).

title: Homework 3 – Regression
text:
2.2 Part b
Compute the estimates we derived using linear algebra in lecture 16: \[\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \left(\mathbf{X}'\mathbf{X}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{X}'\mathbf{Y}.\] Hint: Run ?matrix() in R for a quick reminder about how to create a matrix.



Code
X = matrix(c(rep(1, 5), dat.q2$Temperature), nrow = 5, ncol = 2)
Y = matrix(dat.q2$Strength)

Bhat = solve(t(X)%*%X)%*%t(X)%*%Y
dat.regression = dat.regression |>
  add_row(method = "Linear Algebra", b_0 = Bhat[1], b_1 = Bhat[2])



Using the Linear Algebra approach the regression model we get is \(y = 80.755 + 0.3654x_1\).

title: Homework 3 – Regression
text:
2.3 Part c
Compute the maximum likelihood estimates using optim() in R as described in lecture 16: \[\max_{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma} \mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}=\{\beta_0, \beta_1, \sigma\}).\]



Code
y = dat.q2$Strength
x = dat.q2$Temperature
n = length(y)

ll_theta = function(args){
  b0 = args[1]
  b1 = args[2]
  sd = args[3]
  sum = 0
  for(i in 1:n){
    sum = sum + ((y[i]-(b0+b1*x[i]))^2)/(2*sd^2)
  }
  theta = -((-n/2)*log(2*pi)-(n/2)*log(sd^2)-sum)
}

theta = optim(c(78, 0.5, 1), ll_theta)
dat.regression = dat.regression |>
  add_row(method = "Log Likliehood", b_0 = theta$par[1], b_1 = theta$par[2])



Using the log likliehood method the computed regression is \(y = 80.7449173 + 0.3653252x_1\)

title: Homework 3 – Regression

3.1 Part a
Fit the model predicting MFAP4 using Fibrosis.Stage. Write out the resulting estimate model and interpret the coefficients.



Code
mod.q3 = lm(MFAP4 ~ Fibrosis.Stage, dat.mfap4)



\[
\hat{y} = 9.23 + 1.3x_1 + 3.15x_2 +11.74x_3 + 15.39x_4
\]
In the regression model above \(y\) represents MFAP4 level, the intercept represents the baseline MFAP4 levels, someone with stage 0 fibrosis. \(x_1\) through \(x_4\) represent the stages of fibrosisis, if the patient has fibrosis stage \(n\) then \(x_n\) is 1 and the rest are 0. The coefficients represent how much MFAP4 levels are predicted to increase from the intercept (baseline) based on the observed fibrosis stage.

Adittionaly the qqplot on the left shows the deviation increasing exponentially. In this case it makes sense to do a log transformation because the relationship looks like it could be exponential.

3.5 Part e
Fit the model predicting log(MFAP4) using Fibrosis.Stage, Age, and Gender. Use the natural log, and not the \(\log_2(\cdot)\) recorded in the data file. Write out the resulting estimate model and interpret the coefficients.



Code
mod3.q3 = lm(log(MFAP4) ~ Fibrosis.Stage + Age + Gender, dat.mfap4)



\[
\hat{y} = 1.52 + 0.13x_1 + 0.21x_2 + 0.6x_3 + 0.83x_4 + 0.01x_5 -0.14x_6
\] \[
x_1 = \text{Fibrosis Stage 1}\\
x_2 = \text{Fibrosis Stage 2}\\
x_3 = \text{Fibrosis Stage 3}\\
x_4 = \text{Fibrosis Stage 4}\\
x_5 = \text{Age}\\
x_6 = (\text{Gender == Male})
\]
For this model since we have multiple variables of different types, the intercept is predicted \(\log{\text{MFAP4}}\) value when an individual is fibrosis stage \(0\), age \(0\), and gender female. The next \(4\) coefficients are the increase in predicted \(\log{\text{MFAP4}}\) value based on fibrosis stage, fibrosis stage \(n\) would correspond to \(x_n\) being \(1\) and the other fibrosis variables being \(0\). The sixth coefficient, \(\beta_5\), is the increase in predicted \(\log{\text{MFAP4}}\) value for an increase of one year of age. The last coefficient, \(\beta_6\) is the increase (or in this case decrease) in predicted \(\log{\text{MFAP4}}\) value if the individual is a male.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
Part a
Complete the following steps in \(R=1000\) simulations.

Simulate data for \(k=5\) samples \(n=30\) drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution.
Use pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method="none") to compute unadjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.
Use rstatix::tukey_hsd(...) to compute the Tukey’s HSD adjusted pairwise tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.

In the end, describe the Type I error rates.



Code
n = 30
k = 5
R = 1:1000


significance.dat = tibble(simulation = R, unadjusted = rep(NA, 1000), adjusted = rep(NA, 1000))

for(i in R){
  dat = tibble(
    value = rnorm(n * k),
    group = as.factor(rep(1:k, each = n))
  )
  unadjusted = pairwise.t.test(dat$value, dat$group, p.adjust.method = 'none')
  adjusted = rstatix::tukey_hsd(dat, value ~ group)

  significance.dat$unadjusted[i] = any(unadjusted$p.value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
  significance.dat$adjusted[i] = any(adjusted$p.adj < 0.05)
}

t1.unadj = length(which(significance.dat$unadjusted == TRUE))/length(R)
t1.adj = length(which(significance.dat$adjusted == TRUE))/length(R)



This simulation resulted in a type 1 error of \(28.2\%\) for the unadjusted t-tests, and a type 1 error. of \(5.2\%\) for the adjusted t-tests. This makes sense because without adjusting for Family Wise Error Rate (FWER) we expect the error rate to be \(\alpha \times k\) (\(0.05\times 5 = 0.30\)), which is exactly what we see in the simulation. When adjusting we expect the FWER to be \(\alpha\), and in this case the adjusted rate is approximately \(\alpha = 0.05\).

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
Part b
Redo the simulation, changing to adjust according to the false discovery rate p.adjust.method="BH" and comment on the differences.



Code
n = 30
k = 5

BH = rep(NA, 1000)

R = 1:1000
for(i in R){
  dat = tibble(
    value = rnorm(n * k),
    group = as.factor(rep(1:k, each = n))
  )
  bhadjust = pairwise.t.test(dat$value, dat$group, p.adjust.method = 'BH')

  BH[i] = any(bhadjust$p.value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
}

t1.BH = length(which(BH == TRUE))/length(R)



Running the simulation again while using the ‘BH’ adjust method yields a type 1 error of \(4.4\%\) which is what we would expect for the adjusted FWER.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
Part a
Assume the researchers were targeting a moderate effect size of Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\), setting significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) and desired power \(1 - \beta = 0.80\). Were they adequately powered?
Note: The actual effect size is \(f=0.55\), but researchers usually do not know that ahead of time and defaulted to moderate, instead of specifying a large effect.
What is the required sample size per group (\(n\)) and the overall total sample size (\(N\))? Write the R code using the pwr package to calculate this sample size. This package assumes all samples are of the same size so \(N=nk\), where \(k\) is the number of samples. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.



Code
library(pwr)
k = 5
f = 0.25
alpha = 0.05

The project was funded by several agencies. Suppose that a funding agency suggested funding limiting the researchers to \(N=150\). Evaluate this suggestion in the context of the ANOVA. Would that be large enough to be adequately powered?
Compute the non-centrality parameter \[\lambda = k \cdot n \cdot f^2\] and use the non-central \(F\) distribution to compute the power under \(H_a\) for Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\). Calculate the statistical power achieved under this budget constraint. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.

N = 150
k = 5
n = N/k
f = 0.25

lambda = N*(f^2)

F = qf(0.95, k-1, N-k)

f.dat = tibble(f = seq(0, 10, length.out = 1000)) |>

Visualizing Power using F-distributions




This graph shows the central F-distribution with parameters \(\text{df}_1 = 4\) and \(\text{df}_2 = 145\) and the non central F-distribution with the same degrees of freedom and non centrality parameter \(\lambda = 9.38\), calculated for an effect size \(f = 0.25\). Using the critical F calculated in the code above (\(F_{\textit{critical}} = 2.43\)), the graph displays the power, and the type 1 and 2 errors if the total sample size were \(N = 150\).


By computing the non centrality parameter \(\lambda = 9.38\), and the critical F statistic \(F_{\textit{critical}} = 2.43\), I was able to compare the central F-distribution with the noncentral F-distribution which we assume is the population distribution. With \(\alpha = 0.05\) and effect size \(f = 0.25\), the expected power for a sample size \(N = 150\) is \(0.67\). This is not sufficient because it is less than the desired power \(0.8\)

Explain why the sample size computed in Part a may not be enough and use PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test() to compute a sample size that attains adequate power.
Note: The researchers would have had to do this a priori. Because we aren’t medical experts, you can use sample estimates using the original data. \[\begin{align*}
  n & = \text{answer from part a}\\
  \mu_{\Delta} & = 0.25 \\

\end{align*}\]

n = 30
k = 5

power1 = PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test(n = n, groups = k, delta = 0.25, within.var = 0.77^2)$power
power = 0

while(power < 0.8){

Power of the Pairwise Comparison as n Increases




This graph shows the power of a pairwise test between stages 1 and 2 as the group sample size increases. There is a significant difference in the sample size needed for adequate power between the overall ANOVA F-test and the pairwise test. Shown in red is the sample size required for the overall ANOVA test, and shown in green is the desired power (\(0.8\)). As you can see the with \(n = 30\) the power of the pairwise test is only \(0.07\) and at power \(= 0.8\) the sample size would have to be \(n = 243\).


The sample size originally calculated in part a (\(n = 30\)) may not be enough for the pairwise comparison because the overall ANOVA test tests the if all 5 means are the same, but the pairwise test compares only two means. Thus, more data would be required to test the difference of two means. Using PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test from the I calculated that a sample size of \(n = 243\) is required to achieve power \(= 0.8\). This is greater than \(8\) times the sample size calculated in part a.

Write a short paragraph directly addressing the researcher’s hypothesis using your work in (a)-(d).
The researchers hypothesized that low doses of nicotine could counteract age-related metabolic decline. To measure this they looked at age-induced inflammatory glucose hypermetabolism (\(\text{SUV}_{\text{max}}\)). Their data met the conditions for an ANOVA test, and the results of the test showed that there is a difference in the means of \(\text{SUV}_{\text{max}}\) in different age groups of mice and the treatment group. The second post-hoc test, a pairwise test among groups, revealed that there is a significant difference between \(\text{SUV}_{\text{max}}\) levels among age groups 2M, 6M, and 16M. Since these comparisons yielded a p-value less than \(0.05\) and had power greater than \(0.80\), we can conclude that \(\text{SUV}_{\text{max}}\) increases with age. These results provide support for the researchers hypothesis.

title: Can Dogs Learn Words by Overhearing
text:
Binomial Test

Trials and Conditions
Dror et al. (2026) performed two new-toy trials per dog, still \(n=10\), and each dog chose the correct toy on the first try for each trial. The researchers assume that the probability that the dog chooses the new toy by chance is \(50\%\).
For us to consider the binomial distribution to represent this data we must meet the \(4\) conditions of using the binomial distribution: Binary outcomes, Independent trials, Number of trials fixed, and Same probability of success (BINS). The possible outcomes of the performed trials are either the dog successfully chooses the new toy (\(1\)) or they do not (\(0\)), so the binary condition is met. The trials are independent and performed on separate dogs so the independence condition is met. The number of trials is fixed (\(n=10\)) and each trial is assumed to have the same probability of success (\(50\%\)). Since all conditions are met for the binomial distribution it makes sense to do a binomial test on this data.


Exact Binomial Test
For this test the data used was number of successes \(x=10\) and number of trials \(n=10\). When performing this test the researchers assume that the population parameter, the probability a dog will choose the correct toy the first time, is \(p=50\%\). Below are my hypotheses:
\[
H_0:  p = 50\% \newline
H_a: p \neq 50\%
\]





A graph of the binomial distribution with parameters \(n=10\) and \(p=0.5\) with the observation \(x=10\)



From this graph we can see the binomial distribution for random variable with probability \(p=0.5\) and \(n=10\) trials. For a two-sided test with a confidence level of \(95\%\) the rejection region falls on the interval \(0\leq x\geq 2\) and \(8\leq x\geq 10\). The observation made by researchers, \(x=10\), is the maximum possible observation and lies on the farthest end of the rejection region, indicating a low probability of being observed if the population parameter \(p\) is actually \(50\%\).



Test Results
After performing the exact binomial test on the data with a confidence level of \(95\%\), the probability of observing \(10\) successes out of \(10\) trials is \(\approx0.00195\). Since the observed \(p\)-value is much less than \(\alpha = 0.05\), we can reject the null hypothesis and say that there is statistically discernible evidence that the probability of the dogs choosing the correct toy on the first try is not \(50\%\).



Gaussian Approximation of Binomial Distribution
For sufficiently large samples, \(n\geq30\), we can use the Gaussian approximation of the binomial distribution changing the parameters to:
\[
n = 10, p = 0.5 \newline
\mu_0 = np, \sigma_0=\sqrt{(np(p-1))}
\]





A graph of the Gaussian approximation of the binomial distribution with the observation \(x=10\)



The Gaussian approximation looks very similar to the exact distribution, but there are slight differences. Because the sample size is small and this model is just an approximation, the rejection region begins at a decimal value, however our data is discrete so I rounded towards the edges of the distribution for the rejection region. Even with this smaller rejection region, however, the result is the same, the observation of \(100\%\) successes is in this region.



Test Results
Calculating the probability of the researchers’ observation using the approximate distribution yielded a \(p\)-value of \(\approx0.00443\). Even though the approximated \(p\)-value is more than \(2\times\) larger than the exact (\(\approx0.00195\)), the conclusion of the tests are the same: reject the null.



Inference
In the case of this specific experiment where all trials were successes, I think it is fair to make an inference based on the tests performed due to how low the \(p\)-values are. Both the exact binomial test and the Gaussian approximation produce \(p\)-values well below the significance level of \(\alpha = 0.05\), providing strong evidence against the null hypothesis that the probability of a successful trial is \(p = 0.5\). Therefore, the null hypothesis can be rejected in favor of the conclusion that the probability of success differs from chance. Although the Gaussian approximation produces a larger \(p\)-value than the exact binomial test, both methods lead to the same statistical conclusion. The difference between the two \(p\)-values is likely due to the small sample size (\(n=10\)) and the observed result being at the extreme end of the distribution. For this reason, the exact binomial test provides the more reliable inference for these data.
